title: Pharmacodynamic effects and pharmacokinetics of a new HMG‐CoA reductase inhibitor, rosuvastatin, after morning or evening administration in healthy volunteers

sections.abstract: <jats:p><jats:bold>Aims </jats:bold> To compare the lipid‐regulating effects and steady‐state pharmacokinetics of rosuvastatin, a new synthetic hydroxy methylglutaryl‐coenzyme A (HMG‐CoA) reductase inhibitor, following repeated morning and evening administration in volunteers with fasting serum low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C) concentrations < 4.14 mmol l<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Methods </jats:bold> In this open‐label two‐way crossover trial 24 healthy adult volunteers were randomized to receive rosuvastatin 10 mg orally each morning (07.00 h) or evening (18.00 h) for 14 days. After a 4 week washout period, volunteers received the alternative regimen for 14 days. Rosuvastatin was administered in the absence of food.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Results </jats:bold> Reductions from baseline in serum concentrations of LDL‐C (−41.3%[morning]<jats:italic>vs</jats:italic>−44.2%[evening]), total cholesterol (−30.9%<jats:italic>vs</jats:italic>−31.8%), triglycerides (−17.1%<jats:italic>vs</jats:italic>−22.7%), and apolipoprotein B (−32.4%<jats:italic>vs</jats:italic>−35.3%) were similar following morning and evening administration. AUC(0,24 h) for plasma mevalonic acid (MVA), an <jats:italic>in vivo</jats:italic> marker of HMG‐CoA reductase activity, decreased by −29.9% (morning) <jats:italic>vs</jats:italic>−32.6% (evening). Urinary excretion of MVA declined by −33.6% (morning) <jats:italic>vs</jats:italic>−29.2% (evening). The steady‐state pharmacokinetics of rosuvastatin were very similar following the morning and evening dosing regimens. The <jats:italic>C</jats:italic><jats:sub>max</jats:sub> values were 4.58 <jats:italic>vs</jats:italic> 4.54 ng ml<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>, and AUC(0,24 h) values were 40.1 <jats:italic>vs</jats:italic> 42.7 ng ml<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup> h, following morning and evening administration, respectively. There were no serious adverse events during the trial, and rosuvastatin was well tolerated after morning and evening administration.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Conclusions </jats:bold> The pharmacodynamic effects and pharmacokinetics of rosuvastatin are not dependent on time of dosing. Morning or evening administration is equally effective in lowering LDL‐C<jats:italic>.</jats:italic></jats:p>
